scams.name: Arrecife Airport (ACE) & Puerto del Carmen Taxi Overcharge
scams.description: Lanzarote's César Manrique-Lanzarote Airport (ACE) is a package-holiday hub for UK, German, and Irish tourists headed to the island's three resort strips: Puerto del Carmen, Costa Teguise, and Playa Blanca. Licensed taxis operate on a tariff system; the legitimate fare to Puerto del Carmen is approximately €18–€22, Costa Teguise €25–€30, and Playa Blanca €50–€60 — with a supplement for luggage and night rides. One traveler wrote: 'Upon arrival he charged us about €10 more than the taximeter, which was very blurry' — the blurry-meter scam is the canonical overcharge pattern in Lanzarote. Community reports also document the capacity problem: 'There is never taxis available for up to two hours most nights. The phone line is terrible and never picks up' — meaning peak-time scarcity creates the pressure point where unlicensed or overcharging operators thrive. On payment, travelers advise: 'A lot of taxis accept card, but I would ask when you're entering just to be sure. We always keep cash for taxis' — card refusal is a red flag for the overcharge variant where drivers claim the card machine is 'broken' and demand cash at a higher rate. For older travelers arriving on a package holiday with luggage, the practical defense: (1) confirm the approximate fare before boarding (€18–€22 to Puerto del Carmen, €25–€30 to Costa Teguise, €50–€60 to Playa Blanca); (2) insist on the meter and note the 'modo' setting (modo 1 = day rate, modo 2 = night/weekend rate); (3) photograph the taxi license number from the rear windscreen; (4) if the driver claims the card machine is 'broken' and demands cash, ask for a printed receipt — legitimate drivers issue receipts regardless of payment method; (5) for late-night returns from nightlife, pre-book through your resort's reception rather than hailing on the street.
scams.avoidance: Confirm approximate fare before boarding: €18–€22 Puerto del Carmen, €25–€30 Costa Teguise, €50–€60 Playa Blanca Insist on the meter and note the 'modo' setting (modo 1 = day, modo 2 = night/weekend) Photograph the taxi license number from the rear windscreen on entering Request a printed receipt regardless of payment method — legitimate drivers always issue them For late-night returns from nightlife, pre-book through resort reception rather than hailing on the street
scams.location: César Manrique-Lanzarote Airport (ACE) taxi rank, Puerto del Carmen resort-strip taxi pickups, late-night return rides from nightlife districts

scams.name: Rental Car 'Scratch Scam' & Post-Return Damage Claims
scams.description: Lanzarote's rental-car economy is central to the holiday — the island's geography demands a car for any exploration beyond your resort. This concentration of rentals produces the same 'scratch scam' damage-claim pattern documented in Bilbao and across Spain: a post-return claim for pre-existing or invented damage, typically €150–€400, backed by low-resolution photos sent weeks after the return. One traveler wrote: 'They literally completely scammed me — we rented a car with them because our hotel recommended them but they quoted a post-return damage charge' the victim disputes. Travelers also recommend: 'Auto Reisen at Lanzarote Airport have great cars and great service' — the community has specific operator recommendations to avoid the scam. The scam genre operates across: (1) budget aggregators (Goldcar, Centauro) with low base rates and surprise post-return charges; (2) hotel-recommended 'local' operators that pay commissions and provide lower-quality vehicles; (3) pre-existing minor scratches attributed to the renter at return. The defensive moves are identical to the Bilbao scam: video walk-around at pickup, photograph all four sides, check undercarriage via wheel-well camera, dispute damage claims with credit card chargeback. Community-vetted operators include Cicar car rental (locally owned, high reputation) and Auto Reisen (airport-based, quality service). For older travelers on a Lanzarote package holiday, the protective playbook: (1) use Cicar or Auto Reisen rather than budget aggregators; (2) at pickup, video a walk-around narrating visible marks before signing; (3) photograph every side, roof, wheels, and undercarriage (via phone camera through wheel well); (4) decline collision-damage-waiver upsell at the counter if your credit card provides car-rental insurance; (5) on return, video the returned vehicle and note the drop-off time; (6) for any post-return damage claim, dispute with your credit card within 48 hours using your photo/video evidence; (7) avoid hotel-recommended 'local' operators in favor of independently-reviewed companies.
scams.avoidance: Use community-vetted operators: Cicar or Auto Reisen rather than budget aggregators (Goldcar, Centauro) At pickup, video a walk-around narrating visible marks before signing paperwork Photograph every side, roof, wheels, and undercarriage via phone camera through wheel well Decline collision-damage-waiver upsell if your credit card provides car-rental insurance On return, video the returned vehicle and dispute any post-return damage claim with your credit card within 48 hours
scams.location: Arrecife Airport rental desks (Europcar, Sixt, Avis, Hertz, Goldcar, Centauro), resort-strip rental offices, hotel-recommended 'local' rental agencies

scams.name: Timanfaya National Park Excursion Package Upsells
scams.description: Timanfaya National Park — Lanzarote's Mars-like volcanic landscape — is the island's must-visit natural attraction, and its excursion economy follows the Spain-wide pattern of official vs inflated-reseller pricing. The official bus tour through the Route of the Volcanoes is €12 per adult at the park entrance (timanfaya.com or via public-bus access from Tías). Hotel-concierge excursion desks bundle Timanfaya into 'North Lanzarote' or 'Island Highlights' day trips at €45–€80 per person including transport and a mediocre lunch — for experiences that cost €20–€30 independently. Travelers note: 'Some say it's worth it only if you sit on the right side of the bus' — meaning the €12 official bus tour has its own criticisms, but it remains far better value than packaged alternatives. Community reports also highlight that 'We really wanted to do the Tremesana route in Timanfaya, but it's fully booked' — the Tremesana route (€15 per adult) is the ranger-guided walking tour and must be booked 2–3 months ahead in summer at timanfaya.com directly. Packages that promise 'skip-the-line' Tremesana access for €60+ are marked-up versions of what you can book for free. One traveler summed up the rule: if you go direct to the park, the official bus tour is always available. Travelers also flag the 'camel ride' upsell scam — the ride at the park entrance is €12 per adult and takes 20 minutes; tour-package versions inflate this to €40+. For older travelers on a Lanzarote package holiday, the practical alternative: (1) book the Tremesana route 2–3 months ahead at timanfaya.com (€15 per adult, free for residents) — the best-value Timanfaya experience; (2) for the standard Route of the Volcanoes bus tour, show up at the park entrance and pay €12 per adult; (3) skip hotel-concierge 'Timanfaya excursion' packages at €45–€80 per person; (4) the camel ride at the park entrance is €12 per adult — do not pre-book via hotel at €40+; (5) check the park's official sunrise/sunset volcano demonstration schedule at timanfaya.com to time your visit well.
scams.avoidance: Book Tremesana route 2–3 months ahead at timanfaya.com (€15 per adult — best value) For standard Route of the Volcanoes bus tour, show up at park entrance and pay €12 per adult Skip hotel-concierge 'Timanfaya excursion' packages — the standalone park experience is cheaper and flexible For the camel ride, pay €12 at the park entrance — never pre-book via hotel Combine Timanfaya with Jameos del Agua and Cueva de los Verdes independently for ~€35 total rather than €100+ packaged
scams.location: Timanfaya National Park entrance, hotel-concierge excursion desks, tout stalls at Puerto del Carmen and Playa Blanca, bundled day-trip packages

scams.name: All-Inclusive Resort Drink & Dining Upsells
scams.description: Lanzarote's all-inclusive resort economy is significant — many UK and Irish travelers book a week-long package with 'all-inclusive' food and drink. The scam genre is not outright fraud but a layered set of upsell pressures that turn an 'all-inclusive' holiday into a premium-priced one: (1) 'premium bar' menus at €8–€12 per cocktail (spirit brands not covered by the all-inclusive tier); (2) à-la-carte restaurant 'reservations' requiring an additional €20–€40 per person above the all-inclusive; (3) spa and beach-chair 'packages' at €30–€60 per day above the standard resort offering. Community reports capture the travelers' rights debate: 'We actually tend to do that when we go on holiday: avoid all-inclusive and get half board, or even just breakfast' — half-board is the community-recommended alternative to avoid the upsell pressure. One traveler wrote: 'We stayed in an all inclusive in Lanzarote,' followed by a description of upsell pressure. Travelers frame the broader cost-inflation context and include negative Lanzarote resort experiences, with 2025 family-travel planning tips that specifically warn about Lanzarote all-inclusive upsells. For older travelers booked on an all-inclusive Lanzarote package, the practical defense: (1) read the resort's drinks and dining contract before arrival — identify which spirits, wines, and à-la-carte restaurants are actually included; (2) decline 'premium bar' upsells on arrival — they are non-essential for a good holiday; (3) eat at the standard all-inclusive restaurants rather than paying the €20–€40 à-la-carte supplement; (4) for beach chairs and umbrellas, verify if they are included before paying — some resorts charge extra; (5) skip spa packages pre-booked via the resort concierge at €60+ when comparable services are available in Puerto del Carmen village at €30. Recommended community view: half-board is often better value than all-inclusive for Lanzarote, with local Puerto del Carmen restaurants offering dinner at €15–€25 per person honest pricing.
scams.avoidance: Read the resort's drinks and dining contract before arrival — identify included brands and restaurants Decline 'premium bar' upsells on arrival — standard all-inclusive bar is sufficient for most tastes Eat at standard all-inclusive restaurants rather than paying à-la-carte supplements Verify beach-chair and umbrella inclusion before paying any supplement Skip resort spa packages — comparable services in Puerto del Carmen village are 50% cheaper
scams.location: Puerto del Carmen, Costa Teguise, and Playa Blanca all-inclusive resorts — premium bar menus, à-la-carte restaurant reservations, spa upsells

scams.name: Service Station Fuel & Damage Rip-Offs
scams.description: Lanzarote has a documented service-station scam genre that primarily targets rental-car drivers on the return trip to Arrecife Airport. One traveler wrote of a €500 dispute: 'I think I got scammed out of $500' in a service-station interaction where additional unexpected charges were applied. The scam vectors: (1) pump switching — the attendant fills from a higher-grade fuel nozzle than selected and charges the premium rate; (2) 'forgot to zero' — the previous customer's charge rolls over onto your bill; (3) 'oil top-up' — the attendant offers to top up oil, pours a thin amount, and charges €25+ for the 'service'; (4) damaged-windscreen claims — a post-rental-return 'stone-chip' claim on a windscreen that was fine at drop-off. The worst variant is the rental-car return fuel check: drivers are required to return with a full tank, and some rental operators charge €10–€30 per litre if the tank is even slightly below full. Budget aggregators (Goldcar, Centauro) are particularly known for this. Community reports include Lanzarote operators in the broader Spanish scam pattern and recommend Cicar specifically because their fuel policy is 'same to same' (return with the same level as pickup) rather than 'full to full.' For older travelers on a Lanzarote rental-car holiday, the practical defense: (1) at any service station, watch the pump counter reset to zero before fuel flows; (2) verify the fuel grade matches the nozzle used (regular 95 vs premium 98); (3) decline 'oil top-up' or 'windscreen wipe' offers at pump; (4) before returning the rental, fill the tank at the airport-proximate service station (Repsol at LZ-2/LZ-20 junction is the standard); (5) photograph the fuel gauge reading at full before returning, and retain the fuel receipt; (6) for 'same to same' fuel policies (Cicar), photograph the pickup gauge at the start of the rental.
scams.avoidance: Watch the pump counter reset to zero before fuel flows Verify the fuel grade matches the nozzle used (regular 95 vs premium 98) Decline 'oil top-up' or 'windscreen wipe' offers at pump Before rental return, fill at the airport-proximate Repsol station (LZ-2/LZ-20 junction) Photograph the fuel gauge at full before returning and retain the fuel receipt
scams.location: Service stations along LZ-1 and LZ-2 highways, Arrecife city-center fuel stations, rental-car-return fuel checks

scams.name: Puerto del Carmen & Playa Blanca Restaurant & Beach-Strip Overcharging
scams.description: Lanzarote's resort strips (Puerto del Carmen, Playa Blanca, Costa Teguise) have built the classic 'tourist menu' economy along their seafront promenades — laminated-English photo menus, touts actively recruiting passing tourists, menus without posted prices, and cover charges added to final bills. The overcharging is moderate rather than extreme (prices inflated 30–60% rather than the 200–400% seen in Barcelona's Gothic Quarter), but it is pervasive. Travelers offer the locals-first view: 'In my experience, Spanish companies and businesses don't try to scam you. It's a refreshing change from the UK' — meaning the resort-strip tourist-menu overcharging is the exception, not the Lanzarote norm, with most businesses operating honestly outside the package-tourism corridors. The resort-strip-specific patterns: (1) 'English breakfast' at €12–€15 when an equivalent locals-restaurant breakfast is €5–€7; (2) 'Paella for two' at €35–€45 when a Canary Islands family restaurant paella is €18–€24 per person; (3) cover charges €2–€4 per person not disclosed at seating; (4) beach-chair rentals at €8–€12 per day when municipal chairs are €4–€5 or free; (5) watersport 'package' upsells pushing multiple activities at inflated rates. Community reports frame the broader Spanish resort-tourist-trap context and document negative Lanzarote resort-strip experiences. For older travelers on a package holiday, the practical alternative: (1) walk one street back from the seafront promenade in Puerto del Carmen to find local tapas bars (Calle Roque del Este has community-recommended spots); (2) eat at the all-inclusive resort's standard restaurants rather than seeking 'local' dining on the seafront strip; (3) rent beach chairs at the municipal chiringuito rather than hotel-affiliated vendors; (4) for authentic Canarian food, visit Haría, Teguise, or La Graciosa — the inland and quieter villages have honest-pricing restaurants with papas arrugadas, mojo rojo, and gofio.
scams.avoidance: Walk one street back from the seafront promenade for local tapas bars — Puerto del Carmen's Calle Roque del Este is community-recommended Eat at the all-inclusive resort's standard restaurants rather than seeking 'local' on the seafront strip Rent beach chairs at municipal chiringuitos rather than hotel-affiliated vendors (€4–€5 vs €8–€12) For authentic Canarian food, visit Haría, Teguise, or La Graciosa inland villages Check drink prices — above €4 for a caña/vino tinto is resort-tourist pricing
scams.location: Puerto del Carmen Avenida de las Playas restaurant strip, Playa Blanca marina, Costa Teguise Avenida del Jablillo, hotel-adjacent beach-chair and watersport vendors
